docs.title: Home
docs.text:
This is a modern Cookiecutter template that can be used to initiate a Python project with all the necessary tools for development, testing, and deployment. It supports the following features:

  • uv for dependency management
  • Supports both src and flat layout.
  • CI/CD with GitHub Actions
  • Pre-commit hooks with pre-commit
  • Code quality with ruff, pyright/ty/mypy and deptry.
  • Publishing to PyPI by creating a new release on GitHub
  • Testing and coverage with pytest and codecov
  • Documentation with MkDocs
  • Compatibility testing for multiple versions of Python with tox-uv
  • Containerization with Docker or Podman
  • Development environment with VSCode devcontainers
  • Data versioning and ML pipelines with DVC
  • Changelog in Keep a Changelog format, wired into the agent instructions
  • Optional instructions for configuring AI coding agents (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, or .github/copilot-instructions.md)

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
First, install uv if you haven't already:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

Then, navigate to the directory where you want to create your project and run:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
uvx cookiecutter https://github.com/samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter.git

uvx cookiecutter https://github.com/samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter.git

Or if you prefer using pip:

pip install cookiecutter
cookiecutter https://github.com/samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter.git

Follow the prompts to configure your project. Once completed, a new directory containing your project will be created. Then navigate into your newly created project directory and follow the instructions in the README.md to complete the setup of your project.

docs.title: Acknowledgements
docs.text: This project is partially based on Audrey Feldroy's great cookiecutter-pypackage.

docs.title: Live Demo Guide
docs.text:
This guide provides a 5-minute live demonstration script for showcasing the cookiecutter template. It's designed for audiences who may not be Python experts.

Quick Start

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
uvx cookiecutter gh:samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter --no-input
cd example-project && git init && git add . && make install

uvx cookiecutter gh:samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter --no-input
cd example-project
git init
git add .
uv sync
uv run pre-commit install

docs.title: Before the Demo
docs.text:
macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
# Clean up any previous demo
rm -rf /tmp/example-project

# Navigate to a clean directory
cd /tmp

# Clean up any previous demo
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force $env:TEMP\example-project -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

# Navigate to a clean directory
cd $env:TEMP

docs.title: The Story
docs.text:
"Starting a new Python project the right way typically takes hours: setting up testing, linting, documentation, CI/CD, Docker...

This template does it all in 30 seconds."

docs.title: Run the command
docs.text:
macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
uvx cookiecutter gh:samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter

uvx cookiecutter gh:samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter

docs.title: Answer the prompts
docs.text:
Press Enter to accept defaults, or pause on key prompts to explain:

Prompt Explanation author Your name goes in all the right places - README, LICENSE, pyproject.toml project_name This becomes your folder name and Python package name layout Flat is simpler, src/ layout is for larger projects include_github_actions Free CI/CD on every push to GitHub dockerfile Ready for containerization with Docker or Podman agent_instructions Instructions for AI coding assistants (Copilot, Codex, Claude, Cursor)

Tip

Press Enter rapidly through the prompts to show how quick it is!

docs.title: Show the structure
docs.text:
macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
cd example-project
tree -L 2 -a --dirsfirst

cd example-project
tree /F

Or for a cleaner view, use:

Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Depth 2 | Select-Object FullName

One command gave us a complete project structure - 23 files across 9 directories.

docs.title: Highlight key files
docs.text:
macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
# Show the main code file
cat example_project/__init__.py

# Show the test
cat tests/test_foo.py

# Show the pyproject.toml (modern Python standard)
head -30 pyproject.toml

# Show the main code file
Get-Content example_project\__init__.py

# Show the test
Get-Content tests\test_foo.py

# Show the pyproject.toml (modern Python standard)
Get-Content pyproject.toml -TotalCount 30

Your package is ready to import. Tests are already set up and passing. All dependencies and tool configs in one place - the modern Python way.

docs.title: Part 3: Everything Works Out of the Box
Initialize git and install dependencies
docs.text:
macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
git init && git add .
make install

git init
git add .
uv sync
uv run pre-commit install

Git is required for the pre-commit hooks. uv installs everything in seconds - it's 10-100x faster than pip.

docs.title: Run the tests
docs.text:
macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
make test

uv run python -m pytest --cov --cov-config=pyproject.toml --cov-report=xml

Tests pass with coverage reporting included.

docs.title: Run code quality checks
docs.text:
macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
make check

uv lock --locked
uv run pre-commit run -a
uv run mypy
uv run deptry .

Linting, type checking, and dependency checking - all configured and passing.

Note

The first run may auto-fix minor formatting issues - that's the pre-commit hooks doing their job!

docs.title: Show the Makefile
docs.text:
macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
cat Makefile

Get-Content Makefile

Everything is documented. New team members can get started immediately.

docs.title: Show GitHub Actions
docs.text:
macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
cat .github/workflows/main.yml

Get-Content .github\workflows\main.yml

Push to GitHub and CI runs automatically - tests, linting, everything.

docs.title: Show the documentation site
docs.text:
macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
make docs

uv run mkdocs serve

Your documentation site is ready at localhost:8000.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
What we created in 30 seconds would normally take hours:

  • Dependency management with uv
  • Testing setup with pytest and coverage
  • Code quality tools (ruff, mypy, deptry)
  • CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions
  • Documentation site with MkDocs
  • Docker support
  • AI assistant instructions (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, .github/copilot-instructions.md)

All following best practices, all working together.

docs.title: Recovery Commands
docs.text:
If something goes wrong:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
# Start fresh
cd /tmp && rm -rf example-project

# Skip prompts with defaults
uvx cookiecutter gh:samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter --no-input

# Quick setup after generation
cd example-project && git init && git add . && make install

# Start fresh
cd $env:TEMP
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force example-project -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

# Skip prompts with defaults
uvx cookiecutter gh:samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter --no-input

# Quick setup after generation
cd example-project
git init
git add .
uv sync
uv run pre-commit install

docs.title: Presentation Tips
docs.text:
1. Increase font size - Terminal should be readable from the back of the room
  2. Pre-type long commands - Copy/paste from this guide
  3. Pause after each section - Let the output sink in
  4. Have backup - Keep a pre-generated project ready in case of network issues

docs.title: Migrating Existing Projects
docs.text: Have an existing Python project and want to adopt the best practices from this template? This guide covers your options.

docs.title: Option 1: Cruft (Recommended)
docs.text: Cruft is a tool that links existing projects to cookiecutter templates, allowing you to pull template updates over time.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install cruft
# or
uv tool install cruft

docs.title: Link Your Project
docs.text:
Navigate to your existing project and link it to the template:

cd my-existing-project
cruft link gh:samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter

Cruft will prompt you for the template variables (project name, author, etc.). Answer them to match your existing project.

This creates a .cruft.json file that tracks which template version your project is based on.

docs.title: Check for Updates
docs.text:
See if the template has been updated since you linked:

cruft check

Returns exit code 1 if updates are available (useful for CI).

docs.title: View Changes
docs.text:
See what changed in the template:

cruft diff

docs.title: Apply Updates
docs.text:
Pull template updates into your project:

cruft update

Cruft will show you the changes and ask for confirmation. If there are conflicts with files you've customized, you'll need to resolve them manually (similar to git merge conflicts).

docs.title: Skip Files
docs.text:
Some files shouldn't be updated from the template (e.g., your actual source code, tests, README). Add them to the skip section in .cruft.json:

{
  "template": "gh:samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter",
  "commit": "abc123...",
  "context": {
    "cookiecutter": {
      "project_name": "my-project",
      ...
    }
  },
  "skip": [
    "README.md",
    "src/my_project/**",
    "tests/**"
  ]
}

docs.title: CI Integration
docs.text:
Add a check to your CI pipeline to alert when template updates are available:

# .github/workflows/main.yml
- name: Check for template updates
  run: |
    pip install cruft
    cruft check || echo "::warning::Template updates available. Run 'cruft update' to apply."

docs.title: Option 2: Manual Migration
docs.text: If you prefer not to use Cruft, you can manually adopt template practices:

docs.title: 1. Generate a Reference Project
docs.text:
# Create a fresh project with your settings
uvx cookiecutter gh:samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter -o /tmp/reference

docs.title: 2. Copy Configuration Files
docs.text:
Copy these files from the reference project to yours:

File Purpose pyproject.toml Merge with your existing config Makefile Development commands .pre-commit-config.yaml Code quality hooks .github/workflows/ CI/CD pipelines tox.ini Multi-version testing .python-version Recommended Python version

docs.title: 3. Key Changes Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Migrate from setup.py/setup.cfg to pyproject.toml
  • [ ] Add from __future__ import annotations to all Python files
  • [ ] Set up pre-commit: uv run pre-commit install
  • [ ] Add type hints and configure type checker
  • [ ] Update CI workflows for uv
  • [ ] Add Makefile targets

docs.title: Option 3: Start Fresh
docs.text:
For heavily divergent projects, it may be easier to:

  1. Create a new project from the template
  2. Copy your source code into it
  3. Adjust configurations as needed
# Create new project
uvx cookiecutter gh:samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter

# Copy your code
cp -r old-project/src/* new-project/src/
cp -r old-project/tests/* new-project/tests/

# Install and verify
cd new-project
uv sync
make check && make test

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Approach Effort Future Updates Best For Cruft Medium Automatic Active projects you maintain long-term Manual High Manual One-time adoption, heavily customized projects Start Fresh Low Automatic Small projects, major rewrites

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
1. Commit before migrating - Ensure you can revert if something goes wrong
  2. Run tests after each step - Catch issues early
  3. Review diffs carefully - Don't blindly accept all template changes
  4. Customize .cruft.json skip list - Protect files you don't want overwritten

docs.title: Prompt arguments
docs.text:
When running the command ccp a prompt will start which enables you to configure your repository. The prompt values and their explanation are as follows:

author

Your full name.

email

Your email address.

author_github_handle

Your github handle, i.e. <handle> in https://github.com/<handle>

project_name

Your project name. Should be equal to the name of your repository and it should only contain alphanumeric characters and -'s.

project_slug

The project slug, will default to the project_name with all -'s replaced with _. This will be how you import your code later, e.g.

from <project_slug> import foo

project_description

A short description of your project.

layout

"flat" or "src", defaults to "flat".

  • "flat": Places the Python module in the root directory.
  • "src": Organizes the project by placing the Python module inside a src directory.

Tip for beginners: Choose flat for simplicity. Use src layout if you're publishing a library to PyPI (it prevents accidental imports from the wrong location during development).

minimum_python_version

The oldest Python version the project supports: "3.9" to "3.14", defaults to "3.9". It sets requires-python, the PyPI classifiers, ruff's target-version, the type checker's Python version, and the CI and tox test matrix (every version from the minimum up to 3.14).

Tip for beginners: Choose 3.11 unless you need to support older systems.

development_python_version

The Python version you develop with: "3.9" to "3.14", defaults to "3.14". It is written to .python-version (which uv uses to pick the interpreter) and sets the Docker base image (python:<version>-slim) and the devcontainer image (mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/python:<version>). It must be greater than or equal to minimum_python_version; otherwise project generation fails. Images for Python versions past end-of-life no longer receive updates.

Boolean options on the command line: the true/false options below accept any of true/false, yes/no, y/n, on/off and 1/0, in any case, e.g. uvx cookiecutter gh:samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter --no-input changelog=false dvc=yes. Any other value stops generation with an error.

include_github_actions

true or false. Adds a .github directory with various actions and workflows to setup the environment and run code formatting checks and unittests.

publish_to_pypi

true or false. Adds functionality to the Makefile and Github workflows to make publishing your code as simple as creating a new release release on Github. For more info, see Publishing to PyPI.

deptry

true or false. Adds deptry to the development dependencies of the project, and adds it to the make check command. deptry is a command line tool to check for issues with dependencies in a Python project, such as obsolete or missing dependencies.

mkdocs

true or false. Adds MkDocs documentation to your project. This includes automatically parsing your docstrings and adding them to the documentation. Documentation will be deployed to the gh-pages branch.

codecov

true or false. Adds code coverage checks with codecov.

dockerfile

true or false. Adds a simple Dockerfile.

devcontainer

true or false. Adds a devcontainer specification to the project along with pre-installed pre-commit hooks and VSCode python extension configuration.

dvc

true or false. Adds DVC (Data Version Control) for data versioning, ML pipelines, and experiment tracking. Includes a sample pipeline configuration (dvc.yaml), parameters file (params.yaml), and data directory structure. Ideal for data science and machine learning projects. The pipeline's parameter schema imports pydantic and pyyaml at runtime, so they are added to the project's dependencies; dvc itself (and types-PyYAML when type_checker is mypy) goes in the dev dependency group.

changelog

true or false, defaults to true. Adds a CHANGELOG.md in the Keep a Changelog 1.1.0 format, with an ## [Unreleased] section ready for the first entries. When enabled, the generated agent instruction files and CONTRIBUTING.md remind contributors to log user-facing changes under ## [Unreleased], and the changelog is added to the MkDocs navigation if mkdocs is true. For more info, see Changelog with Keep a Changelog.

type_checker

The type checker to use in the generated project. Supported values are pyright, ty, mypy, and pyrefly. When enabled, the project will include configuration and CI steps (where applicable) to run the selected type checker.

Tip for beginners: Choose pyright — it's fast and has excellent VS Code integration.

agent_instructions

Select which AI coding agent instruction files to include. Options:

  • "suggested" (default): Copilot + Codex — includes both .github/copilot-instructions.md and AGENTS.md
  • "codex": Codex only — includes AGENTS.md
  • "claude": Claude only — includes CLAUDE.md
  • "copilot": Copilot only — includes .github/copilot-instructions.md
  • "cursor": Cursor only — includes .cursorrules
  • "all": All agents — includes all instruction files
  • "none": No agent instructions

include_py_typed

true or false. Includes a py.typed marker file in the package so downstream consumers know the package exposes type information. Recommended for libraries that expose type hints.

Tip for beginners: Leave as true unless you know you don't need it. This only matters if others will import your package as a library.

agent_profile

Select an agent profile from the available options. Choices include minimal and full.

  • minimal: A small, lightweight agent configuration with minimal dependencies and examples.
  • full: A more feature-complete agent configuration with additional example code, documentation, and optional dependencies.

open_source_license

Choose a license. Options: ["1. MIT License", "2. BSD license", "3. ISC license", "4. Apache Software License 2.0", "5. GNU General Public License v3", "6. Not open source"]

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text: This page contains a complete tutorial on how to create your project.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Make sure you have the following set up:

  • [ ] A GitHub account
  • [ ] Git installed on your machine
  • [ ] SSH keys set up for GitHub (guide)
  • [ ] A code editor (we recommend VS Code)
  • [ ] Basic familiarity with the command line

Don't have these yet? No problem! Click the links above to get set up.

docs.title: Step 1: Install uv
docs.text:
uv is a fast Python package manager that replaces pip, virtualenv, and more. This template uses uv to manage dependencies and virtual environments.

To install uv, follow the instructions here or use the commands below:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

docs.title: Step 2: Generate your project
docs.text:
On your local machine, navigate to the directory in which you want to create a project directory, and run the following command:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
uvx cookiecutter https://github.com/samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter.git

uvx cookiecutter https://github.com/samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter.git

For an explanation of the prompt arguments, see Prompt Arguments.

docs.title: Step 3: Set up your Github repository
docs.text: Create an empty new repository on Github. Give it a name that only contains alphanumeric characters and optionally -. DO NOT check any boxes under the option Initialize this repository with.

docs.title: Step 4: Initialize git and install the environment
docs.text:
Run the following commands, replacing <project_name> with the name of your project.

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
cd <project_name>
git init -b main
make install

Windows does not include make by default. You can either install make or run the commands directly:

cd <project_name>
git init -b main
uv sync
uv run pre-commit install

This generates the uv.lock file, which the CI/CD pipeline needs.

docs.title: Step 5: Run the pre-commit hooks
docs.text:
Stage your files and run the pre-commit hooks:

git add .
uv run pre-commit run -a

Note: Pre-commit only checks staged files. Without git add . first, you'll see "no files to check".

If a hook shows "Failed" with "files were modified by this hook", it has fixed the files for you. Stage them in the next step.

docs.title: Step 6: Commit the project
docs.text:
git add .
git commit -m "Init commit"

docs.title: Step 7: Upload your project to Github
docs.text:
Run the following commands, replacing <project_name> with the name that you also gave the Github repository and <github_author_handle> with your Github username.

git remote add origin git@github.com:<github_author_handle>/<project_name>.git
git push -u origin main

docs.title: Step 8: Set up Codecov (optional)
docs.text:
If you enabled codecov for your project:

  1. Sign up at codecov.io with your GitHub account
  2. For private repositories, you'll need to add a CODECOV_TOKEN secret:
    • Go to app.codecov.io and find your repository
    • Copy the repository upload token
    • In GitHub, go to Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions
    • Add a new secret named CODECOV_TOKEN with the token value

For more details, see Codecov setup.

docs.title: Step 9: Configure PyPI publishing (optional)
docs.text: If you want to publish your package to PyPI, see Publishing to PyPI.

docs.title: Step 10: Enable documentation
docs.text:
To deploy your documentation to GitHub Pages:

1. Create a release to trigger the documentation build:

  • Go to your repository on GitHub
  • Click Releases on the right sidebar
  • Click Draft a new release
  • Enter a tag using semantic version format (e.g., 0.1.0, 1.0.0)
  • Add a title and click Publish release

2. Enable GitHub Pages (after the release workflow completes):

  • Go to Settings > Pages
  • Under Source, select the gh-pages branch
  • Your docs will be available at https://<username>.github.io/<project-name>/

docs.title: Step 11: You're all set!
docs.text: That's it! I hope this repository saved you a lot of manual configuration. If you have any improvement suggestions, feel free to raise an issue or open a PR on Github!

docs.title: Windows: Installing Make
docs.text:
If you prefer using make commands on Windows, you can install it via:

ChocolateyScoopwinget 
choco install make

scoop install make

winget install GnuWin32.Make

After installation, restart your terminal and make commands will work as documented.

docs.title: "Not a git repository" error
docs.text:
If you see this when running make install:

❌ Error: Not a git repository. Run 'git init -b main' first.

Solution: Run git init -b main before make install. See Step 4 above.

docs.title: "Permission denied (publickey)" when pushing
docs.text:
If git push fails with a permission error:

git@github.com: Permission denied (publickey).

Solution: Your SSH keys aren't set up correctly. Follow GitHub's SSH guide to configure them.

docs.title: Pre-commit shows "no files to check"
docs.text:
If you see (no files to check)Skipped for all hooks:

Solution: Stage your files first with git add ., then run pre-commit again.

docs.title: "uv: command not found"
docs.text:
If your terminal doesn't recognize uv:

Solution:

  1. Close and reopen your terminal
  2. If still not working, check that uv is in your PATH (see uv installation docs)

docs.title: CI/CD pipeline fails on first push
docs.text:
This is expected! The pipeline fails because:

  1. uv.lock wasn't committed yet
  2. Pre-commit hooks haven't run to fix formatting

Solution: Follow Steps 5-7 in this tutorial to fix formatting and commit the lock file.

docs.title: Copilot Setup Steps workflow fails
docs.text:
If you see the "Copilot Setup Steps" workflow fail on your first push:

This is expected! This workflow is used by GitHub Copilot to set up the development environment. Like the Main workflow, it fails initially because uv.lock doesn't exist yet.

Solution: After completing Steps 5-7 (installing dependencies and committing the lock file), this workflow will pass on subsequent runs.

What is Copilot Setup Steps? This workflow configures the environment for GitHub Copilot Workspace. If you don't use Copilot, you can safely ignore this workflow or delete .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml.

docs.title: Agent Instructions
docs.text: This cookiecutter template can generate instruction files for various AI coding agents. Use the agent_instructions option to select which agents to configure.

docs.title: Available Options
docs.text: Option Files Generated Description suggested (default) AGENTS.md, .github/copilot-instructions.md Copilot + Codex — recommended for most projects codex AGENTS.md OpenAI Codex/ChatGPT instructions claude CLAUDE.md Claude Code instructions copilot .github/copilot-instructions.md GitHub Copilot instructions cursor .cursorrules Cursor editor instructions all All files All agent instruction files none None No agent instructions

docs.title: Agent Profile
docs.text:
You can choose between two detail levels with agent_profile:

  • Minimal: A lightweight version with essential commands and quality gates
  • Full: A comprehensive version with detailed guidelines, project structure, code conventions, and common task workflows

When changelog is true, every generated agent file also tells agents to add an entry under ## [Unreleased] in CHANGELOG.md for user-facing changes. See Changelog with Keep a Changelog.

docs.title: AGENTS.md (Codex)
docs.text:
The AGENTS.md file provides concise, actionable instructions for AI coding agents. This format is recognized by OpenAI's Codex and many other AI assistants. It includes:

  • Environment setup: How to install dependencies using uv
  • Quality gates: Commands to run before proposing changes (formatting, linting, type checking, tests)
  • Conventions: Code style guidelines (line length, docstring formats)
  • PR etiquette: Best practices for pull requests

docs.title: Example AGENTS.md content
docs.text:
# AGENTS.md — rules for coding agents

> This repository follows the uv/Ruff/mypy/pytest stack.

## Environment & install

- Use **uv** for everything.
- Install: `uv sync`
- Run commands with `uv run …`

## Quality gate (do these before proposing changes)

- Format: `uv run ruff format .`
- Lint:   `uv run ruff check .`
- Types:  `uv run mypy .`
- Tests:  `uv run pytest -q`

## PR etiquette

- Small, focused PRs.
- Include/adjust tests and docs.
- Use Conventional Commits in the title.

docs.title: CLAUDE.md (Claude Code)
docs.text:
The CLAUDE.md file provides project-specific guidance for Claude Code (claude.ai/code). It follows Claude's conventions for project instructions and includes:

  • Project overview and technology stack
  • Common commands for development workflow
  • Project structure explanation
  • Code style and type checking requirements
  • Testing guidelines

docs.title: .github/copilot-instructions.md (GitHub Copilot)
docs.text: The .github/copilot-instructions.md file provides detailed guidelines for GitHub Copilot code generation:

docs.title: Project Context & Environment
docs.text:
• Specifies that the project uses uv for dependency management
  • Ensures all Python commands run through the .venv virtual environment

docs.title: Typing & Data Models
docs.text:
• Enforces strong typing with type annotations for all code
  • Prefers @dataclass or Pydantic models over unstructured dictionaries
  • Requires triple-quoted documentation for all dataclass attributes

docs.title: Function & Method Signatures
docs.text:
• Requires explicit type annotations for parameters and return values
  • Uses -> None explicitly for functions without return values

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Generates unit tests alongside implementations
  • Covers both happy-path and error conditions
  • Uses explicit type/attribute assertions

docs.title: .cursorrules (Cursor)
docs.text:
The .cursorrules file provides instructions for the Cursor editor's AI features. It includes:

  • Environment setup with uv
  • Quality gate commands
  • Code conventions (when using the full profile)
  • Project structure overview
  • PR guidelines

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
By configuring agent instructions, you:

  1. Ensure consistency: All AI-generated code follows your project's conventions
  2. Improve code quality: Agents automatically apply best practices and type safety
  3. Reduce review time: Generated code meets quality standards from the start
  4. Accelerate onboarding: New contributors (human or AI) quickly understand the workflow
  5. Maintain standards: Project guidelines are enforced automatically during code generation

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
To configure agent instructions when generating your project:

# Use the suggested combination (Copilot + Codex)
agent_instructions: "suggested"

# Or choose a specific agent
agent_instructions: "claude"

# Choose the detail level
agent_profile: "full"  # or "minimal"

These options can be set when running cookiecutter, or configured in your cookiecutter.json defaults.

docs.title: Changelog with Keep a Changelog
docs.text: If changelog is set to true (the default), the generated project includes a CHANGELOG.md that follows the Keep a Changelog 1.1.0 format. Recording changes as they land, rather than reconstructing them from commit history at release time, gives contributors, release tooling and AI coding agents a single place to read and update.

docs.title: What's Included
docs.text:
The generated CHANGELOG.md starts with:

  • The standard Keep a Changelog header, linking to keepachangelog.com and Semantic Versioning
  • An ## [Unreleased] section with an ### Added entry for the initial project scaffold
  • An [Unreleased] link reference pointing at the commit history of the main branch on GitHub, since no releases exist yet
# Changelog

All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

## [Unreleased]

### Added

- Initial project scaffold generated from [project-kit-cookiecutter](https://github.com/samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter).

[Unreleased]: https://github.com/<handle>/<project_name>/commits/main

docs.title: Integration with Other Options
docs.text:
When changelog is true:

  • Agent instructions: every generated agent file (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .github/copilot-instructions.md, .cursorrules) tells agents to add an entry under ## [Unreleased] for user-facing changes. The minimal agent_profile keeps this to one line; the full profile adds a short example.
  • CONTRIBUTING.md: the pull request guidelines include a reminder to update CHANGELOG.md under [Unreleased].
  • MkDocs: if mkdocs is true, a Changelog page is added to the docs navigation. It includes the root CHANGELOG.md with the pymdownx.snippets extension, so there is only one file to maintain.

When changelog is false, none of these files or rules are generated.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Keep a Changelog groups entries under these categories, in this order:

Category Use for Added New features Changed Changes in existing functionality Deprecated Features that will be removed in an upcoming release Removed Features removed in this release Fixed Bug fixes Security Fixes for vulnerabilities

A few rules keep the file useful:

  • Write entries for people using the project, not for the commit log. Internal refactors, test and CI changes usually do not need an entry.
  • Add new entries under ## [Unreleased], creating the category heading if it is missing.
  • When cutting a release, rename ## [Unreleased] to ## [x.y.z] - YYYY-MM-DD, add a fresh empty ## [Unreleased] section above it, and update the link references at the bottom of the file:
## [Unreleased]

## [0.1.0] - 2026-01-15

### Added

- Initial project scaffold generated from [project-kit-cookiecutter](https://github.com/samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter).

[Unreleased]: https://github.com/<handle>/<project_name>/compare/0.1.0...HEAD
[0.1.0]: https://github.com/<handle>/<project_name>/releases/tag/0.1.0

docs.title: CI/CD with Github actions
docs.text:
When include_github_actions is set to true, a .github directory is added with the following structure:

.github
├── actions
│   └── setup-python-env
│       └── action.yml
├── workflows
│   ├── main.yml
│   ├── on-release-main.yml
│   ├── validate-codecov-config.yml
│   └── copilot-setup-steps.yml
└── copilot-instructions.md

main.yml is triggered on pushes to main and on pull requests. It runs quality checks (linting, formatting, type checking) and tests across multiple Python versions (3.9-3.14). The workflow uses the setup-python-env action to set up the environment with uv.

on-release-main.yml is triggered whenever a new release is published. It publishes the project to PyPI if publish_to_pypi is set to true, and it builds and deploys the documentation if mkdocs is set to true. To learn more about these features, see Publishing to PyPI and Documentation with MkDocs.

validate-codecov-config.yml validates the codecov configuration file (only included if codecov is set to true).

copilot-setup-steps.yml provides setup steps for GitHub Copilot (only included if agent_instructions includes Copilot).

docs.title: How to trigger a release?
docs.text:
To trigger a new release, navigate to your repository on GitHub, click Releases on the right, and then select Draft a new release. If you fail to find the button, you could also directly visit https://github.com/<username>/<repository-name>/releases/new.

Give your release a title, and add a new tag in the form *.*.* where the *'s are alphanumeric. To finish, press Publish release.

docs.title: Test coverage with codecov
docs.text: If codecov is set to true, pytest-cov is added as a development dependency, and make test will run the tests and output a coverage report as coverage.xml.

docs.title: Setting up Codecov
docs.text:
1. Sign up at codecov.io with your GitHub account
  2. Your public repositories should work automatically
  3. For private repositories, you need to add a secret:
    • Go to app.codecov.io and select your repository
    • Copy the "Repository Upload Token"
    • In your GitHub repository, go to Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions
    • Add a new repository secret named CODECOV_TOKEN

For more details on token types, see Codecov's documentation.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
A codecov.yaml file is created with the following defaults:

# Badge color changes from red to green between 70% and 100%
# PR pipeline fails if codecov falls with 1%

coverage:
  range: 70..100
  round: down
  precision: 1
  status:
    project:
      default:
        target: auto
        threshold: 1%

# Ignoring Paths
# --------------
# which folders/files to ignore
ignore:
  - "foo/bar.py"

If codecov is set to false, pytest-cov is not added to the development dependencies and the github actions won't produce a coverage report.

docs.title: Reproducible development environments with VSCode devcontainers
docs.text:
If devcontainer is set to true, the project uses the VSCode devcontainer specification to create a reproducible development environment. The devcontainer is defined in the .devcontainer directory and pre-installs all dependencies from uv required to develop, test and build the project.

The devcontainer also installs the pre-commit hooks and configures the VSCode python extension to use the appropriate python interpretor and pytest paths.

docs.title: Containerization with Docker or Podman
docs.text:
If dockerfile is set to true, a simple Dockerfile is added to the repository. The Dockerfile installs uv, sets up the environment, and runs foo.py when executed.

The container image can be built with:

docker build . -t my-container-image

or, if using Podman:

podman build . -t my-container-image

It can then be run in the background with:

docker run -d my-container-image

or, if using Podman:

podman run -d my-container-image

Alternatively, run it in interactive mode with:

docker run --rm -it --entrypoint bash my-container-image

or, if using Podman:

podman run --rm -it --entrypoint bash my-container-image

docs.title: Data Version Control with DVC
docs.text: If dvc is set to True, the generated project includes DVC (Data Version Control) for versioning data, models, and creating reproducible ML/data pipelines.

docs.title: What's Included
docs.text:
When you enable DVC, the following files are created:

File/Directory Purpose .dvc/ DVC configuration directory .dvc/config DVC settings (remote storage configuration) .dvcignore Patterns for files DVC should ignore dvc.yaml Pipeline definition with example stages params.yaml Pipeline parameters file <package>/schemas/params.py Pydantic schema for params.yaml validation <package>/schemas/params.schema.json JSON schema for VS Code validation data/raw/ Directory for raw input data data/processed/ Directory for processed/transformed data <package>/prepare.py, <package>/train.py, <package>/evaluate.py Example pipeline scripts

docs.title: 1. Configure Remote Storage
docs.text:
DVC supports multiple storage backends. Configure your preferred remote:

Amazon S3Google Cloud StorageAzure Blob StorageLocal/Network Path 
uv run dvc remote add -d storage s3://mybucket/dvc-storage

uv run dvc remote add -d storage gs://mybucket/dvc-storage

uv run dvc remote add -d storage azure://mycontainer/dvc-storage

# Local directory
uv run dvc remote add -d storage /path/to/storage

# Network/SSH path
uv run dvc remote add -d storage ssh://user@server/path/to/storage

Recommended Setup

Contact your team for the recommended remote storage configuration for your organization's projects.

docs.title: 2. Add Your Data
docs.text:
Place your raw data in data/raw/, then track it with DVC:

# Add a single file
uv run dvc add data/raw/your-dataset.csv

# Or add an entire directory
uv run dvc add data/raw/

# Commit the tracking files to git
git add data/raw.dvc data/.gitignore
git commit -m "Add raw dataset"

docs.title: 3. Run the Pipeline
docs.text:
Execute all pipeline stages:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
make dvc-repro

uv run dvc repro

docs.title: 4. Push Data to Remote
docs.text:
After running your pipeline, push data and outputs to your remote:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
make dvc-push

uv run dvc push

docs.title: 5. Pull Data (for collaborators)
docs.text:
Team members can pull data from the remote:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
make dvc-pull

uv run dvc pull

docs.title: Makefile Commands
docs.text: Command Description make dvc-repro Run DVC pipeline (reproduces all stages) make dvc-pull Pull data from DVC remote make dvc-push Push data to DVC remote make dvc-status Show DVC pipeline status make dvc-dag Show DVC pipeline DAG visualization

docs.title: Machine Learning Workflows
docs.text:
DVC excels at versioning ML experiments:

  • Dataset versioning: Track different versions of training data alongside your code
  • Model versioning: Version trained models without bloating your git repository
  • Experiment tracking: Compare metrics across experiments with dvc metrics diff
  • Reproducibility: Anyone can reproduce your exact results with dvc repro

Example workflow: 

# Train a model
uv run dvc repro

# Check metrics
uv run dvc metrics show

# Compare with previous run
uv run dvc metrics diff

docs.title: Data Pipelines / ETL
docs.text:
DVC also works well for data engineering:

  • ETL pipelines: Define data transformation stages in dvc.yaml
  • Data lineage: Track which raw data produced which outputs
  • Incremental processing: DVC only reruns stages when dependencies change
  • Collaboration: Share large datasets without storing them in Git

Example pipeline flow: 

data/raw/ → prepare stage → data/processed/ → transform stage → data/final/

docs.title: GitHub Actions Integration
docs.text:
When include_github_actions is enabled, the CI pipeline includes a dvc-pipeline job that:

  1. Pulls data from your configured remote (if available)
  2. Verifies the pipeline is reproducible with dvc repro --dry

docs.title: Required Secrets
docs.text:
Configure these repository secrets for cloud storage access:

Provider Secrets Required AWS S3 AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY GCP GCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY (JSON content) Azure AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT, AZURE_STORAGE_KEY

To add secrets:

  1. Go to your repository → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions
  2. Click "New repository secret"
  3. Add each required secret for your storage provider

docs.title: Pipeline Structure
docs.text:
The default dvc.yaml includes a sample pipeline:

stages:
  prepare:
    cmd: uv run python your_package/prepare.py
    deps:
      - data/raw
      - your_package/prepare.py
    params:
      - prepare
    outs:
      - data/processed

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
• cmd: The command to run for this stage
  • deps: Files/directories this stage depends on (triggers rerun if changed)
  • params: Parameters from params.yaml (triggers rerun if changed)
  • outs: Output files/directories (cached and tracked by DVC)
  • metrics: JSON/YAML files with metrics (for experiment comparison)
  • plots: Visualization files

docs.title: Extending the Pipeline
docs.text:
Add more stages by uncommenting or adding to dvc.yaml:

stages:
  prepare:
    # ... existing stage ...

  train:
    cmd: uv run python your_package/train.py
    deps:
      - data/processed
      - your_package/train.py
    params:
      - train
    outs:
      - models/model.pkl
    metrics:
      - metrics/train_metrics.json:
          cache: false

  evaluate:
    cmd: uv run python your_package/evaluate.py
    deps:
      - models/model.pkl
      - data/processed
    metrics:
      - metrics/eval_metrics.json:
          cache: false

docs.title: Parameter Schema Validation
docs.text: Pipeline parameters are validated using Pydantic to catch configuration errors early.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. <package>/schemas/params.py defines Pydantic models for all pipeline parameters
  2. <package>/schemas/params.schema.json provides JSON schema for VS Code validation
  3. Pipeline scripts use PipelineParams.from_yaml() to load and validate parameters

docs.title: Adding New Parameters
docs.text:
When modifying params.yaml, you must also update the schema:

  1. Edit <package>/schemas/params.py to add/modify Pydantic models
  2. Regenerate the JSON schema: 
    uv run python -c "from <package>.schemas import PipelineParams; PipelineParams.generate_json_schema()"
  3. Commit both params.yaml and the updated schema files

docs.title: Example: Adding a New Parameter
docs.text:
# In <package>/schemas/params.py
class TrainParams(BaseModel):
    epochs: int = Field(default=10, ge=1)
    learning_rate: float = Field(default=0.001, gt=0.0)
    batch_size: int = Field(default=32, ge=1)
    # Add new parameter:
    dropout: float = Field(default=0.5, ge=0.0, le=1.0, description="Dropout rate")

Then update params.yaml: 

train:
  epochs: 10
  learning_rate: 0.001
  batch_size: 32
  dropout: 0.5  # New parameter

docs.title: VS Code Integration
docs.text:
With the Red Hat YAML extension installed, VS Code provides:

  • Autocomplete for parameter names
  • Validation against the schema
  • Hover documentation from field descriptions

The extension is included in .vscode/extensions.json recommendations.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Commit .dvc files: Always commit the .dvc tracking files to Git
  2. Use meaningful stage names: Make your pipeline self-documenting
  3. Parameterize everything: Put hyperparameters in params.yaml for easy experimentation
  4. Track metrics: Use metrics: in dvc.yaml for experiment comparison
  5. Document dependencies: List all file and parameter dependencies explicitly
  6. Use cache: false for metrics: Keeps metrics files in the repo for easy comparison
  7. Keep schema in sync: Always update schemas/params.py when changing params.yaml

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• DVC Documentation
  • DVC Pipelines Guide
  • DVC Remote Storage
  • DVC Experiments
  • DVC with CI/CD

docs.title: Linting and code quality
docs.text:
Code can be linted and quality-checked with the command

make check

Note that this requires the pre-commit hooks to be installed.

This command will run the following tools:

docs.title: ruff
docs.text:
ruff is used to lint and format the code, and it is configured through pyproject.toml:

[tool.ruff]
target-version = "py39"
line-length = 120
fix = true

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = [
    "YTT",   # flake8-2020
    "S",     # flake8-bandit
    "DTZ",   # flake8-datetimez
    "LOG",   # flake8-logging
    "PIE",   # flake8-pie
    "PT",    # flake8-pytest-style
    "RET",   # flake8-return
    "TC",    # flake8-type-checking
    "PTH",   # flake8-use-pathlib
    "B",     # flake8-bugbear
    "A",     # flake8-builtins
    "C4",    # flake8-comprehensions
    "T10",   # flake8-debugger
    "SIM",   # flake8-simplify
    "I",     # isort
    "C90",   # mccabe
    "E", "W",  # pycodestyle
    "F",     # pyflakes
    "PGH",   # pygrep-hooks
    "UP",    # pyupgrade
    "RUF",   # ruff
    "TRY",   # tryceratops
    "PERF",  # perflint
    "FURB",  # refurb
]
ignore = [
    "E501",  # LineTooLong
    "E731",  # DoNotAssignLambda
]
# Let TC fixes add `from __future__ import annotations` instead of quoting types
future-annotations = true

[tool.ruff.lint.per-file-ignores]
"tests/*" = ["S101"]

[tool.ruff.format]
preview = true

The rule families beyond the core pyflakes/pycodestyle/isort set are taken from the ones Ruff itself enables by default since v0.16 (datetimes, logging, pytest style, pathlib, performance, refurb and type-checking imports). Because the template sets an explicit select, upgrading Ruff never changes which rules run in your project.

Formatter preview mode only opts into the two styles Ruff still marks as preview since its 2026 style guide (v0.15): fluent method-chain layout and bracket hugging. Remove preview = true if you prefer the stable style only.

docs.title: mypy
docs.text:
mypy is used for static type checking, and it's configuration can be edited in pyproject.toml.

[tool.mypy]
disallow_untyped_defs = true
disallow_any_unimported = true
no_implicit_optional = true
check_untyped_defs = true
warn_return_any = true
warn_unused_ignores = true
show_error_codes = true
exclude = [
    '\.venv',
    '{{cookiecutter.project_name}}',
    'tests'
]

docs.title: ty
docs.text:
ty is an extremely fast type checker (and language server) that can be used instead of mypy, and it's configuration can be edited in pyproject.toml.

[tool.ty.environment]
python = "./.venv"
python-version = "3.9"

[tool.ty.terminal]
error-on-warning = true

ty is still in beta (0.0.x), and its defaults and diagnostics can change between releases. The template therefore pins an exact version (ty==0.0.94) in the dev dependency group; bump it deliberately. ty has no single strict preset: tune individual rules under [tool.ty.rules].

docs.title: pyrefly
docs.text:
Pyrefly is a fast type checker and language server from Meta that reached a stable 1.0 in 2026. The template enables its strict preset, because without a preset Pyrefly only runs a minimal set of checks.

[tool.pyrefly]
project-includes = ["example_project", "tests"]
python-version = "3.9"
preset = "strict"

If you are migrating an existing mypy project, uv run pyrefly init converts a [tool.mypy] configuration.

docs.title: pyright
docs.text:
pyright is a fast type checker for Python created by Microsoft. It's the type checker that powers Pylance in VS Code. Configuration can be edited in pyproject.toml.

[tool.pyright]
pythonVersion = "3.9"
typeCheckingMode = "strict"

docs.title: deptry
docs.text: deptry is used to check the code for dependency issues, and it can be configured by adding a [tool.deptry] section in pyproject.toml. For more information, see this section documentation of deptry.

docs.title: Github Actions
docs.text: If include_github_actions is set to true, code formatting is checked for every merge request, every merge to main, and every release.

docs.title: Makefile
docs.text:
The generated repository will have a Makefile available. A list of all available commands can be obtained by running make help in the terminal.

Windows Users

Windows does not include make by default. You have two options:

  1. Install make via Chocolatey, Scoop, or winget (see Installing Make on Windows)
  2. Run the underlying commands directly (shown in the table below)

docs.title: Available Commands
docs.text:
Initially, if all features are selected, the following commands are available:

Make Command Direct Command (Windows-friendly) Description make install uv sync && uv run pre-commit install Install the uv environment and pre-commit hooks make check See check commands Lint and check code make test uv run python -m pytest --cov --cov-config=pyproject.toml --cov-report=xml Test the code with pytest make build uvx --from build pyproject-build --installer uv Build wheel file make clean-build uv run python -c "import shutil; import os; shutil.rmtree('dist') if os.path.exists('dist') else None" Clean build artifacts make publish uvx twine upload --repository-url https://upload.pypi.org/legacy/ dist/* Publish a release to PyPI make docs-test uv run mkdocs build -s Test documentation build make docs uv run mkdocs serve Build and serve documentation make docker-build docker build -t <project_name>:latest . Build Docker image make docker-run docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 <project_name>:latest Run Docker container make dvc-repro uv run dvc repro Run DVC pipeline (if dvc enabled) make dvc-pull uv run dvc pull Pull data from DVC remote (if dvc enabled) make dvc-push uv run dvc push Push data to DVC remote (if dvc enabled) make dvc-status uv run dvc status Show DVC pipeline status (if dvc enabled) make dvc-dag uv run dvc dag Show DVC pipeline DAG visualization (if dvc enabled)

docs.title: Check Command Breakdown
docs.text:
The make check command runs multiple quality checks in sequence:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
make check

Run these commands in order:

# Check lock file consistency
uv lock --locked

# Run pre-commit hooks (linting, formatting)
uv run pre-commit run -a

# Run type checker (mypy or ty, depending on your choice)
uv run mypy
# or: uv run ty check

# Run deptry (if enabled)
uv run deptry .

docs.title: Installing Make on Windows
docs.text:
If you prefer using make commands, install it via one of these package managers:

ChocolateyScoopwinget 
choco install make

scoop install make

winget install GnuWin32.Make

After installation, restart your terminal and make commands will work as documented.

docs.title: Documentation with MkDocs
docs.text:
If mkdocs is set to true, documentation of your project is automatically added using MkDocs. Next to that, if include_github_actions is set to true, the documentation is automatically deployed to your gh-pages branch, and made available at https://<github_handle>.github.io/<project_name>/.

To view the documentation locally, simply run

make docs

This command will generate and build your documentation, and start the server locally so you can access it at http://localhost:8000.

docs.title: Enabling the documentation on GitHub
docs.text:
To enable your documentation on GitHub, first navigate to Settings > Actions > General in your repository, and under Workflow permissions select Read and write permissions

Then, create a new release for your project.

Then, in your repository, navigate to Settings > Code and Automation > Pages. If you succesfully created a new release, you should see a notification saying Your site is ready to be published at https://<author_github_handle>.github.io/<project_name>/.

To finalize deploying your documentation, under Source, select the branch gh-pages. Your documentation should then be live within a few minutes.

docs.title: Documenting docstrings
docs.text:
The generated project also converts all your docstrings into legible documentation. By default, the project is configured to work with google style docstrings.

An example of a Google style docstring:

def function_with_pep484_type_annotations(param1: int, param2: str) -> bool:
"""Example function with PEP 484 type annotations.

Args:
    param1: The first parameter.
    param2: The second parameter.

Returns:
    The return value. True for success, False otherwise.

For more examples, see here.

docs.title: Node (TypeScript) template
docs.text: project-kit-cookiecutter also holds a template for TypeScript libraries, in the node/ folder of the repository. It applies the same standards as the Python template (linting and formatting through pre-commit, a Keep a Changelog CHANGELOG.md, agent instructions, GitHub Actions, a license choice and a devcontainer) to a Node project.

docs.title: Generate a project
docs.text:
Pass the folder with --directory:

uvx cookiecutter https://github.com/samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter.git --directory node

With cruft, so the project can be updated later:

uvx cruft create https://github.com/samuelduchesne/project-kit-cookiecutter.git --directory node

The project-kit plugin's new-project workflow does this for you when you ask for a Node project.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
Concern Tool Package manager pnpm, pinned in packageManager (install pnpm with npm install -g pnpm; it switches to the pinned version. Node.js 25 and later no longer include corepack) Language TypeScript, strict, ES modules; tsc builds dist/ with type declarations Tests Vitest with V8 coverage Linting and formatting Biome, run by a local pre-commit hook with the project's own Biome version Other hooks The Python template's generic pre-commit hooks (merge conflicts, YAML, JSON, end of file, trailing whitespace) CI make check and a test-and-build matrix from the chosen Node version up

make install installs the dependencies and the pre-commit hooks, make check runs the lockfile, pre-commit and type checks, make test runs the tests and make build compiles. The pre-commit hooks run with uvx, so contributors need uv as well as Node and pnpm.

Commit pnpm-lock.yaml after the first make install: CI installs with --frozen-lockfile.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Effect project_name example-project Folder and npm package name: lowercase letters, digits and -, starting with a letter node_version 24 Minimum Node version (engines), .nvmrc, devcontainer image and the lowest CI version; 22 and 26 are also offered include_github_actions true .github/workflows/main.yml codecov true Coverage upload in CI, codecov.yaml and the badge publish_to_npm false .github/workflows/release.yml, which publishes to npm with provenance when a GitHub release is published; otherwise the package is private devcontainer true .devcontainer/devcontainer.json changelog true CHANGELOG.md and the changelog rule in the agent files and CONTRIBUTING.md agent_instructions, agent_profile suggested, minimal Same as the Python template, see Agent Instructions open_source_license MIT license LICENSE and the license field (UNLICENSED for "Not open source")

docs.title: Publishing to npm
docs.text: The release workflow uses npm trusted publishing: no token is stored in the repository. Before the first release, add the repository and the release.yml workflow as a trusted publisher of the package on npmjs.com. Then bump the version (npm version <major|minor|patch> --no-git-tag-version), commit, push, and publish a GitHub release whose tag matches the version (1.2.0 or v1.2.0).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: When publish_to_pypi is set to true, the on-release-main.yml workflow automatically publishes your package to PyPI whenever you create a new release.

docs.title: Set up PyPI Token
docs.text:
Before your first release, add your PyPI API token as a GitHub secret:

  1. Get your PyPI token:

    • Go to PyPI Account Settings
    • Scroll to "API tokens" and click "Add API token"
    • Give it a name (e.g., "GitHub Actions")
    • Set scope to "Entire account" (or project-specific after first publish)
    • Copy the token (starts with pypi-)

  2. Add to GitHub:

    • Go to your repository → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions
    • Click "New repository secret"
    • Name: PYPI_TOKEN
    • Value: paste your token
    • Click "Add secret"

docs.title: Testing with TestPyPI (Recommended)
docs.text:
Before publishing to the real PyPI, test your setup with TestPyPI:

  1. Get a TestPyPI token:

    • Create an account at test.pypi.org
    • Go to Account Settings → "Add API token"
    • Copy the token

  2. Modify workflow for testing:

    Edit .github/workflows/on-release-main.yml, add UV_PUBLISH_URL:

    - name: Publish package
  run: uv publish
  env:
    UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.PYPI_TOKEN }}
    UV_PUBLISH_URL: https://test.pypi.org/legacy/  # Remove after testing

  3. Add TestPyPI token as PYPI_TOKEN secret (temporarily)

  4. Create a test release and verify at https://test.pypi.org/project/your-package/

  5. Switch to real PyPI:

    • Remove the UV_PUBLISH_URL line from the workflow
    • Update PYPI_TOKEN secret with your real PyPI token

docs.title: Publishing from your local machine
docs.text:
Not recommended, but possible:

make build-and-publish

docs.title: Unittesting with Pytest
docs.text:
pytest is automatically added to the environment. There will be a template unittest in the tests directory upon creation of the project, which can be run with

make test

pytest runs in strict mode, so typos in markers or config options and unexpectedly passing xfail tests fail the run instead of being silently ignored. With a minimum Python of 3.10 or newer the template uses pytest 9's single strict = true option:

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
strict = true

pytest 9 requires Python 3.10, so projects with a 3.9 minimum get the equivalent pytest 8 options:

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
addopts = ["--strict-markers", "--strict-config"]
xfail_strict = true

If include_github_actions is set to true, the tests are automatically run for every merge request, every merge to main, and every release.

docs.title: Security Features
docs.text: This cookiecutter template implements a defense-in-depth security architecture with multiple layers of protection enabled by default. Every generated project ships with industry-standard security tooling configured and enforced.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Layer Tool/Feature Protection Static Analysis Ruff + Bandit (S rules) Vulnerability detection Type Safety pyright/mypy/ty (strict) Type confusion prevention Dependency Security uv lock + deptry Supply chain protection Pre-commit Hooks 8+ validation hooks Input sanitization CI/CD GitHub Actions Automated enforcement Containers Docker slim images Minimal attack surface

docs.title: Static Security Analysis with Bandit
docs.text:
The template enables comprehensive security scanning via Ruff's flake8-bandit integration. The "S" rules are enabled by default in pyproject.toml:

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = [
    "S",        # flake8-bandit - security scanner
    # ... other rules
]

docs.title: What Bandit Detects
docs.text:
Bandit scans for common security vulnerabilities including:

Rule Range Category Examples S101-S113 General Assert in production, exec(), hardcoded passwords S301-S324 Cryptography Insecure pickle, weak hashes (MD5, SHA1), insecure random S501-S509 Network SSL/TLS validation disabled, HTTP without TLS S601-S612 Injection Shell injection, SQL injection, code injection S701-S703 Templates Jinja2 autoescape disabled, Django XSS

docs.title: Example Detections
docs.text:
# S105: Hardcoded password - DETECTED
password = "secret123"

# S608: SQL injection - DETECTED
query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = {user_id}"

# S301: Insecure pickle - DETECTED
data = pickle.loads(untrusted_data)

# S324: Insecure hash - DETECTED
hashlib.md5(data)

Test Exemption

Only S101 (assert usage) is exempted in tests. All other security rules remain enforced.

docs.title: Type Safety
docs.text:
Strict type checking prevents type confusion attacks and ensures data validation:

pyright (default)mypyty 
[tool.pyright]
pythonVersion = "3.9"
typeCheckingMode = "strict"

[tool.mypy]
disallow_untyped_defs = true
disallow_any_unimported = true
no_implicit_optional = true
check_untyped_defs = true
warn_return_any = true

[tool.ty.environment]
python-version = "3.9"

docs.title: Security Benefits
docs.text:
• Type confusion prevention: Catches mismatched types that could lead to vulnerabilities
  • Input validation: Forces explicit type declarations on function boundaries
  • Data flow tracking: Warns when Any types bypass validation

docs.title: Locked Dependencies
docs.text:
The template uses uv with locked dependencies to prevent supply chain attacks:

# Verified in CI/CD
uv lock --locked

This ensures:

  • No unexpected dependency upgrades
  • Reproducible builds across environments
  • Protection against dependency injection attacks

docs.title: Dependency Auditing with Deptry
docs.text:
When deptry is enabled (default), it scans for:

  • Unused dependencies: Reduces attack surface
  • Obsolete packages: Flags deprecated libraries
  • Missing dependencies: Catches incomplete requirements
make check  # Includes deptry scan

docs.title: Pre-commit Security Hooks
docs.text:
The .pre-commit-config.yaml includes validation hooks that run before every commit:

repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    hooks:
      - id: check-yaml          # Prevents YAML injection
      - id: check-toml          # Validates TOML syntax
      - id: check-json          # Validates JSON syntax
      - id: check-merge-conflict # Detects unresolved conflicts

  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit
    hooks:
      - id: ruff-check          # Security + linting rules
      - id: ruff-format         # Consistent formatting

docs.title: Security Value
docs.text:
• Prevents malformed configuration files that could bypass security controls
  • Enforces consistent formatting (malicious code is harder to hide)
  • Validates all structured data formats before commit

docs.title: GitHub Actions Hardening
docs.text:
The generated workflows follow security best practices:

# Pinned action versions (not @latest)
- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- uses: actions/cache@v4

# Secrets via environment variables
env:
  CODECOV_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}

docs.title: Security Controls
docs.text: Practice Implementation Pinned versions All actions use specific versions (v4, v5) Secret isolation Credentials via GitHub Secrets, never in code Multi-version testing Python 3.9-3.14 matrix testing Mandatory checks make check must pass before merge

docs.title: .gitignore Protection
docs.text:
The template excludes sensitive files by default:

# Environment files
.env
.envrc

# Credentials
.pypirc
.netrc

# Virtual environments
.venv/
venv/

docs.title: CI/CD Secrets
docs.text:
Secrets are managed via GitHub repository settings:

Secret Purpose PYPI_TOKEN PyPI publishing authentication CODECOV_TOKEN Code coverage reporting AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID DVC S3 storage (optional) GCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY DVC GCS storage (optional)

docs.title: Container Security
docs.text:
When dockerfile is enabled, the generated Dockerfile follows security best practices:

# Minimal base image (smaller attack surface)
FROM python:3.14-slim

# Locked dependencies
RUN uv sync --locked

# BuildKit cache mounts (prevents cache poisoning)
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv \
    uv sync --locked

docs.title: Security Features
docs.text:
• Minimal base image: python:3.14-slim has fewer packages to exploit
  • Locked dependencies: --locked flag ensures exact versions
  • No secrets in image: Credentials passed at runtime via environment
  • BuildKit caching: Secure cache management

docs.title: Input Validation
docs.text:
The pre-generation hook validates all user inputs:

# hooks/pre_gen_project.py
PROJECT_NAME_REGEX = r"^[-a-zA-Z][-a-zA-Z0-9]+$"
PROJECT_SLUG_REGEX = r"^[_a-zA-Z][_a-zA-Z0-9]+$"

This prevents:

  • Command injection via malformed project names
  • Path traversal vulnerabilities
  • Invalid Python module names

docs.title: The Security Gate
docs.text:
All security checks are enforced via a single command:

make check

This runs:

  1. uv lock --locked - Dependency consistency
  2. uv run pre-commit run -a - All pre-commit hooks (including Bandit)
  3. uv run pyright (or mypy/ty) - Type checking
  4. uv run deptry . - Dependency audit (if enabled)

CI/CD Enforcement

The make check command runs in CI/CD on every pull request and push to main. Code cannot be merged if any security check fails.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This template provides enterprise-grade security out of the box:

  • OWASP Top 10 coverage via Bandit rules
  • Supply chain protection via locked dependencies
  • Type safety via strict type checking
  • Secret protection via .gitignore and GitHub Secrets
  • Container hardening via minimal images and locked deps
  • Automated enforcement via CI/CD pipelines

All security features are enabled by default and enforced automatically.

docs.title: Compatibility testing with Tox
docs.text:
The generated project uses tox-uv to test compatibility with multiple Python versions. You can run tox locally:

uv run tox

By default, the project is tested with Python 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14.

Testing for compatibility with different Python versions is also done automatically in the CI/CD pipeline on every pull request, merge to main, and on each release.

If you want to test for compatbility with more Python versions you can simply add them to tox.ini and to the separate workflows in .github.

docs.title: Dependency management with uv
docs.text: The generated repository uses uv for its dependency management.

docs.title: Installing uv
docs.text:
If you don't have uv installed yet:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

For more installation options, see the uv documentation.

docs.title: Adding dependencies
docs.text:
When you have created your repository using this cookiecutter template, a uv environment is pre-configured in pyproject.toml. Add your project-specific dependencies with:

uv add <package>

docs.title: Installing the environment
docs.text:
Install the environment with:

uv sync

docs.title: Running commands
docs.text:
You can run commands within your virtual environment using uv run:

uv run python -m pytest

Or activate the virtual environment and run commands directly:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell)Windows (cmd) 
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pytest

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pytest

.venv\Scripts\activate.bat
python -m pytest
